regal.grenzgaenger: Stations that refuse to have a genre.
regal.freakshow: Mashups, vaporwave, genre accidents on purpose.
regal.tiefe: Ambient, drone, outer space. Music to disappear into.
regal.japan: City pop, J-jazz, local radio, community.
regal.barrio: Salsa, cumbia, Latin alternative — from Havana to Buenos Aires.
regal.rueckspiegel: Old times, but the stubborn kind. Italo disco, spacesynth, early rave — what nobody played back then, and even less so now.
regal.fundstuecke: Regional and curious finds from around the world.
regal.klassik: The shelf that depends most on your connection: classical loses more in compression than other music, because quiet passages and overtones go first. Lossless classical streams are rare — what a station delivers is on its card, and where it matters, so is the connection it needs.
regal.jazz: Jazz and what borders on it.
regal.wuehlkiste: Mainstream, clearly marked. What's here is what everyone knows — for visitors looking for something familiar. From here it's just a few shelves to music you've never heard.

sender.nts-1: Since 2011, NTS has broadcast round the clock from a storefront in Dalston, London, with shows from over 600 hosts. No other station moves this casually between Congolese soukous, free jazz, and grime — often within the same hour.
sender.nts-2: NTS's second channel runs quieter than the first, making room for long shows that don't fit anywhere else's grid. If NTS 1 feels too erratic, this is where you'll settle in.
sender.nts-slow-focus: One of NTS's curated endless mixes, assembled from their own archive: ambient, modern classical, and field recordings, no talk. Made for working to, without turning into elevator music.
sender.dublab-la: Since 1999, this non-profit collective in Los Angeles has broadcast whatever it likes — ambient, krautrock, field recordings, often within the same hour. If you want to know what radio without a music desk sounds like, start here.
sender.dublab-bcn: The Spanish offshoot of dublab, run by its own collective in Barcelona. More Mediterranean and more danceable than the mothership in Los Angeles, with plenty of Iberian electronic music you won't hear anywhere else.
sender.dublab-de: The German dublab branch is based in Cologne and broadcasts in German and English, with a strong pull toward jazz and experimental electronic music. The only one of the three dublabs with regular German-language talk.
sender.cashmere: A member-run radio out of a storefront in Berlin-Lichtenberg, carried by volunteers and free of advertising. Shows range from Eastern European folk-music research to noise — held together only by the curiosity of the people on the mic.
sender.kiosk-radio: A converted newsstand in Brussels' Warandepark, broadcasting live since 2017 — DJs literally stand in a booth in the city park. The Belgian scene is more idiosyncratic than the British one, and here's why.
sender.refuge-worldwide: A Neukölln station whose proceeds go to non-profit projects — radio as fundraiser, with first-rate programming. Musically somewhere between club and talk show, often on topics commercial radio wouldn't touch.
sender.rinse-uk: Started in 1994 as a pirate station in a London tower block and was the birthplace of grime and UK garage, before getting an official license in 2010. The shows still sound like someone broadcasting illegally from a rooftop.
sender.rinse-france: The French offshoot of Rinse, with its own programming out of Paris rather than a relay from London. Considerably more Afro house, coupé-décalé, and French rap than the British original.
sender.kool-fm: The oldest jungle pirate station still on air, broadcasting since 1991 and under Rinse's roof since 2022. If you want to know what jungle sounds like played by people who were there, listen here.
sender.wfmu: The longest-running freeform station in the US, listener-funded since 1958 and without any music desk — every host plays whatever they want. Legendary for shows where free jazz is followed by a 1962 advertising record.
sender.yammat-fm: A Croatian independent station broadcasting at 320 kbit/s AAC, which makes it sound better than most major outlets. Programming cuts across funk, soul, Balkan electronic music, and whatever's currently interesting in Zagreb.
sender.neu-radio: A university radio out of Bologna, run by students and local musicians. Italian community radio sounds different from British — chattier, warmer, and with a fondness for things that can go wrong.
sender.radio-nova: The Paris station that has shaped the term Sono Mondiale since 1981: world music before the word existed. Still the best place to hear African funk and French hip-hop side by side.
sender.fip: The public-broadcast eclectic from Paris, on air since 1971 and famous for programming changes that follow no logic at all — Miles Davis, then Aphex Twin, then a chanson. Almost never hosted, never advertised.
sender.rp-main-flac: A married couple in Northern California has hand-assembled every broadcast hour since 2000, funding it all through donations. Broadcasts lossless in FLAC — the difference from 128 kbit/s is clearly audible on good headphones.
sender.rp-world-flac: The world-music channel from the same people, also lossless and also hand-curated. Less rock than the main channel, more from Mali, Brazil, and Turkey instead — without the esoteric aftertaste world music often has.
sender.worldwide-fm: Founded by Gilles Peterson, the British DJ who's been thinking jazz and club music together since the eighties. The programming follows his ear: Brazilian material, broken beat, African jazz, plenty of talk in between.
sender.hirschmilch-techno: A one-man station from Kassel running ad-free and unhosted since 2003. The techno channel is the hardest of the four and holds the line for hours without lapsing into cheap tricks.
sender.hirschmilch-electronic: The broadest of the Hirschmilch channels: electronica, downtempo, IDM, all instrumental and uninterrupted. The channel where, after an hour, you forget radio is even playing — in the best sense.
sender.hirschmilch-hypnotic: The name says it all: repetitive, slowly mutating tracks that take twelve minutes to get anywhere. For work that can't afford distraction, the most useful channel in the whole catalog.
sender.hirschmilch-progressive: Progressive house and trance in the long, patient build that was standard before the festival boom. If you only know trance as a wall of anthems, this is the other, more restrained half of the genre.
sender.bassdrive: The worldwide go-to for drum and bass since 1999, run by a network of volunteer DJs across several continents. No station has held the scene outside Britain together like this one.
sender.brokenbeats: A Ukrainian station for atmospheric drum and bass, broadcasting at over 300 kbit/s AAC — technically one of the best streams in the whole catalog. Has kept running for years, even under conditions that would have shut down others long ago.
sender.frisky: One of the few underground house stations that has made the leap across two decades, on air since 2003. Built on continuous DJ mixes rather than individual tracks — radio structured like a night at the club.
sender.uzic-techno: A Swiss station playing minimal and techno exclusively, favoring the stripped-down, near-austere strain of it. Little build, little drama — but tracks you'd otherwise only find on twelve-inches.
sender.fm4: The alternative channel of Austrian public broadcasting, bilingual in German and English, on air since 1995. A public broadcaster that plays drum and bass and experimental music in the evenings instead of chart hits — Germany has nothing comparable.
sender.ukbass: A small British station for bass music in all its forms — dubstep, garage, bassline, jungle. Small enough that the selection still sounds like people, not playlist software.
sender.atmospheric-dnb: The softer twin channel to Brokenbeats: liquid and atmospheric drum and bass in the same high sound quality. The channel for the hours when the hard variant would be too much.
sender.res-radio: A Russian underground station for electronic music at 320 kbit/s and without any interruption. The selection is idiosyncratic enough that you regularly hear tracks that show up in no Western catalog.
sender.isekoi-chill: A French channel for electronic chill music, broadcasting lossless in FLAC — rare in this genre and immediately audible on good headphones. Musically somewhere between downtempo, lo-fi, and Japanese-influenced electronic music.
sender.dnbfm: A Russian drum and bass station at 320 kbit/s, mapping the Eastern European scene — a world of its own with its own producers. If you know the British strain, this is its considerably rougher relative.
sender.soma-dronezone: The best-known drone channel from listener-funded SomaFM in San Francisco, on air for over twenty years. Ambient without a beat, without structure, without end — meant as a sound space, not a music program.
sender.soma-deepspace: Ambient and space sounds, deeper and colder than Drone Zone, with occasional radio chatter from spaceflight archives. The channel to leave running when the apartment starts feeling too small.
sender.soma-groovesalad: The house's best-known channel, the same steady hand for over twenty years — and lossless as of recently: FLAC around 1000 kbit/s instead of 128 MP3. If you want to know what the difference does, here's the comparison against your own memory.
sender.etx-fm: A small American station for what it calls Electronic Listening Music — ambient, modern classical, and everything in between. No hosting, no advertising, no genre fence.
sender.camp-radio: A French collective broadcasts ambient and experimental music in the Opus format, which sounds noticeably better than MP3 at low bitrates. The selection is calm but never arbitrary — something is always happening.
sender.substrate-radio: Dark ambient and industrial drone from Seattle, considerably more inhospitable than the SomaFM channels. Not a relaxation program, but music that makes a room oppressive — if that's what you're after, there's little better.
sender.deep-in-space: A Russian ambient channel with a leaning toward psychedelic and space-related sounds. The selection follows a different tradition than the American one — more Berlin School, less Californian relaxation.
sender.newage-flac: A Greek station broadcasting new age and meditative music lossless in FLAC — a rarity in this genre. Especially on quiet, overtone-rich pieces, it makes an audible difference.
sender.ambi-nature: A Swiss station mixing ambient with real nature recordings — rain, forest, water, recorded in specific places. Resolved high enough at 320 kbit/s that the quiet details survive.
sender.spokoynoe: Calm radio, as the name says in Russian: instrumental music with no announcements, no advertising, at 320 kbit/s. A quiet corner of the catalog that gets by without the usual relaxation clichés and whale song.
sender.cafedelmar-calm: The calm channel from the bar in Sant Antoni, whose sunset compilations invented the chillout genre starting in 1994. Unlike the thousand imitators, this station has the original records and the sense behind them.
sender.nature-sleep: Very slow, very quiet soundscapes, expressly meant for falling asleep and without any dramatic arc. Paired with the sleep timer, the most useful channel in the catalog for late evening.
sender.adroit-jazz: A New York station playing jazz off original shellac and vinyl records, crackle and all. You actually hear the record, not the remastered reissue — a difference you won't want to miss after two tracks.
sender.classic-vinyl: The sister channel to Adroit Jazz, with recordings from the twenties through the fifties, also straight off the record. Radio as archive visit — tracks here haven't been digitized by anyone in seventy years.
sender.jazz24: The jazz channel of public station KNKX out of Seattle, hosted by people who know their records. At 256 kbit/s AAC, one of the best-sounding jazz streams around, without the elevator-music lean of many smooth jazz stations.
sender.wbgo: The jazz station out of Newark, listener-funded since 1979 and the most important jazz station on the American East Coast. Broadcasts right out of the city where many of the recordings it plays were made.
sender.kjazz-bebop: A specialist channel playing bebop exclusively — Parker, Gillespie, Powell, and their successors, nothing after. That narrowness is the strength: if you want bebop, you don't want to land on fusion after three tracks.
sender.ella-bebop: A small Hamburg jazz station with several specialist channels, this one for bebop and hard bop. German jazz radio has become rare — this one runs without advertising and with palpable expertise.
sender.ashiya-radio: A local station from the small town of Ashiya between Osaka and Kobe, playing a surprising amount of jazz between Japanese local news. Radio from a slice of Japanese everyday life a European would otherwise never hear.
sender.japan-citypop: City pop, wall to wall — that Japanese sound of the late seventies and eighties that combined funk, AOR, and jazz fusion, and has been rediscovered worldwide for a few years now. The direct neighborhood of Atarashii Gakko and their forebears.
sender.listen-moe-jpop: A volunteer-run station for Japanese pop, broadcasting in the Opus format at 256 kbit/s — the best sound quality this genre gets anywhere. The track list is maintained by the listener community, not an editorial desk.
sender.listen-moe-kpop: The Korean sister channel, technically identical and also community-curated. It's here because the line between J-pop and K-pop has long since become musically porous.
sender.radio-nanahira: A tiny station out of the Japanese doujin scene, that half-world of self-published music that never makes it into stores. Opus at 256 kbit/s, and a selection you'll find nowhere else.
sender.gensokyo: Plays exclusively fan arrangements of music from the Touhou game series — a whole musical universe with thousands of albums that almost nobody outside Japan knows. The range runs from metal to jazz, all built on the same melodies.
sender.r-a-d-io: A station that grew out of an imageboard community, where volunteers DJ live and listeners request tracks through a queue. Chaotic, often silly, and precisely for that reason closer to what radio used to be.
sender.fm-setagaya: The district station of Setagaya, a residential area in western Tokyo, with neighborhood news and weather in Japanese. Not a music station, but a window into perfectly ordinary Japanese daily life.
sender.gotanno-fm: A mini-station from Tokyo's Gotanno neighborhood, run by a handful of people from the block. So small that listening feels like overhearing someone in the next room.
sender.jazz-sakura: Japanese jazz, played by Japanese musicians — a scene with its own tradition that's been producing remarkable work since the sixties and gets barely noticed in the West. Calmer and more formal than American jazz.
sender.stereo-anime: Anime theme music from five decades, from the seventies to today. A genre far more musically ambitious than its reputation — here you hear big band arrangements next to synth-pop and metal.
sender.yumico-radio: A French collective broadcasts Japanese music at 256 kbit/s — city pop, Shibuya-kei, video game music, selected with a European eye. The outside perspective turns up different finds than Japanese stations do.
sender.sound-up-nfrs: A regional station from Niigata Prefecture on Japan's west coast, far from Tokyo. Local music, local news — the opposite of the metropolitan perspective that shapes Japanese culture abroad.
sender.anime-para-ti: Anime music with Spanish-language hosting — a station for Latin America's huge, largely overlooked anime community. Two cultures in one program, which regularly leads to surprising transitions.
sender.gladys-coleccion: Alejandra Fierro Eleta has assembled one of the largest private collections of Latin American music in the world and broadcasts from it. Cuban recordings from the forties next to Colombian psychedelic funk — a record store within the record store.
sender.gladys-latinfresh: The present-day channel of the same collection: current Latin American productions instead of archive material. Shows that the traditions aren't sitting in a museum, but are being carried forward electronically right now.
sender.ibero-909: The university radio of the Ibero in Mexico City, run by students and steadfastly avoiding the charts. The best place for Mexican indie, digital cumbia, and whatever's occupying the local scene right now.
sender.colombia-salsadura: Salsa dura is the hard, fast style from the seventies — Fania sound, horn sections, no ballads. Broadcast from Cali, the city that turned salsa into folk art even though it isn't from Colombia.
sender.cumbias-inmortales: Classic cumbia from Mexico, the sonidero tradition of street parties in Monterrey and Mexico City. Music that's been coming out of man-high speakers on street corners there for decades — here without the street noise.
sender.salsa-maestra: A Peruvian salsa station with a pronounced pull toward recordings from the seventies and eighties. Peru has its own salsa history, one that usually gets lost next to Cuba and New York.
sender.salsa-brava-ccs: Venezuelan salsa from Caracas, a city with its own, harder strain of the genre. Broadcasts at 136 kbit/s AAC and without ad breaks, which is the exception among Latin American stations.
sender.cumbia-90s: Bolivian and Andean cumbia from the nineties, with synthesizers and drum machines instead of horns. A branch of the genre all its own, sounding like someone ran folk music through a home studio.
sender.panamericana-salsa: The salsa channel of a major Peruvian station, with real hosting and callers from Lima. Less curated than the other channels on this shelf, but closer to what's actually playing there.
sender.radionica: Colombia's public station for everything else that doesn't make it onto radio — Colombian rock, cumbia in unexpected arrangements, hip-hop out of Medellín. The bitrate is modest; the selection isn't.
sender.bytefm: A listener-funded Hamburg station practicing music journalism in the best sense since 2008: shows with a theme, research, and a point of view instead of a rotation playlist. The closest German counterpart to WFMU.
sender.wdr-cosmo: WDR's world-music channel, grown out of the sixties program for guest workers. Today the best German-language source for global pop, Afrobeats, and Turkish psychedelia.
sender.radio-mega: A free radio from the provinces along the Rhône, part of the French network of independent local stations. Broadcasts at 320 kbit/s with a selection that pays no mind to reach.
sender.ancient-fm: Exclusively medieval and Renaissance music, played on period instruments. A station nobody would think to invent, which is exactly why it exists — for over fifteen years now.
sender.nhyira-fm: A station from Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city, with programming mostly in Twi. Highlife, gospel, and long talk shows in a language almost no European listener understands — and it works anyway.
sender.lagosjump: An online station from Lagos, mapping Nigeria's music scene up close rather than by way of Western charts. Afrobeats sounds different when it hasn't been sorted for export.
sender.yabiladi-chaabi: Chaabi is Moroccan folk music for festivals and weddings, loud, repetitive, and almost unknown in Europe. This station plays it without the soft focus world-music compilations like to apply.
sender.yurd-fm: An Azerbaijani station with mugham, the local modal art music, mixed in with current pop. Music from a region that sits culturally between Persia, Turkey, and Russia and belongs to none of them.
sender.radyo-siran: A small-town station from Şiran in northeastern Anatolia, with Turkish folk music and local news. So small and so local that while listening, you can be fairly sure how many people are tuned in.
sender.bamtaare-fm: A village station from Senegal, broadcasting in Pulaar for the region along the Senegal River. Community radio in its most original form — announcements, music, people passing word to each other.
sender.radio-armisa: An Italian provincial station from the Bergamo countryside with surprisingly good sound quality. Italian pop music away from the Sanremo axis, with local news from a valley almost nobody knows.
sender.nts-field-recordings: Not a music channel, but field recordings throughout: rainforests, subway stations, marketplaces, thunderstorms. The strangest show in the whole catalog, and surprisingly good at changing a room.
sender.bootie-mashup: The people behind the Bootie party series, playing mashups in San Francisco and a dozen other cities since 2003. At 320 kbit/s, with a mixing craft that goes well beyond the usual two-track trick.
sender.nightwave-plaza: Vaporwave around the clock, with stretched-out eighties ad jingles, department-store music, and video-game sounds. An internet culture that materialized as a radio station — animated shopping mall on the website included.
sender.soma-vaporwaves: SomaFM's answer to the vaporwave phenomenon, sorted a bit more accessibly than Nightwave Plaza. For anyone who wants to understand the appeal without fighting straight through the genre's thicket.
sender.kohina: Broadcasting exclusively music from the demoscene and old home computers since 2003 — Amiga modules, C64 sounds, tracker tunes. A genre that shaped a whole generation of programmers and plays nowhere else.
sender.keygen-fm: Plays the chiptune music from software-piracy keygens — small programs whose authors developed a whole music culture out of sheer ambition. Absurd origin, surprisingly good music.
sender.vapor-funk: The danceable offshoot of vaporwave, called future funk: eighties Japanese city pop records, sped up and laid over house beats. Happier than the source material, and considerably faster.
sender.chiptune-247: Modern chiptune productions — new music on old game-console hardware rather than nostalgia reruns. The limit of three channels and noise forces an inventiveness you can hear.
sender.nolife-radio: The remnant of a French niche TV channel for video-game and Japanese culture, living on as radio. Video game music, J-pop, and French oddities in a mix that could only have come about this way.
sender.shmup-radio: Exclusively music from shoot-'em-up arcade games, mostly Japanese ones from the nineties. An extremely narrow genre with surprisingly dense musicianship — horn sections and basslines for games that last nine minutes.
sender.gamesboro: Video game music from four decades, from orchestral scores to 8-bit tracks, run by a Vienna collective. A repertoire that by now fills serious concert halls and still barely shows up on radio.
sender.soma-sf1033: Ambient soundscapes with actual San Francisco police radio mixed underneath — calls, codes, street names, all live. Sounds like the soundtrack to a movie being shot outside right now.
sender.soma-missioncontrol: Ambient with spaceflight radio traffic mixed in — Apollo, Space Shuttle, mission control. The voices are real, pulled from NASA archives, giving the music a gravity that pure space ambient never reaches.
sender.soma-sonicuniverse: The channel where jazz and electronic music collide without either swallowing the other — nu jazz, free jazz, broken beat. Filed under Border-crossers because it fits neither drawer.
sender.soma-suburbsofgoa: Indian classical and Bollywood finds, woven together with downtempo and dub — a genre mix that exists nowhere else quite like this. Neither world music nor electronic, but a third thing with no name.
sender.soma-illstreet: Exotica and space-age bachelor-pad music from the fifties and sixties — the records postwar suburbs used to dream of Tahiti. Absurd, kitschy, and musically surprisingly sophisticated.
sender.soma-tikitime: The even more specialized twin of Illinois Street Lounge: tiki culture, Hawaiian guitars, bird calls between tracks. A genre that comes straight out of American cocktail bars and is entirely made up.
sender.soma-7soul: Exclusively soul and R&B off original seven-inch singles from the fifties and sixties, straight off the record. The format restriction is the curation — whatever never came out as a single doesn't play here.
sender.soma-bootliquor: Americana and alt-country for people who can't do anything with Nashville — raw, thinly produced, often from labels nobody's heard of. At 320 kbit/s, the best-sounding channel the house has.
sender.soma-thistle: Celtic music and its relatives around the world — from Scottish ballads through Breton dance music to Canadian fiddle. Shows how far a tradition can travel when emigrants take it with them.
sender.soma-doomed: Dark ambient and horror-film sounds, expressly meant to be spooky and originally built for Halloween. The most unsettling channel in the catalog — which is sometimes exactly right.
sender.soma-cliqhop: IDM in the Warp Records tradition: chopped-up rhythms, glitches, tracks that refuse to hold a beat. A genre whose heyday is behind it and is kept alive here.
sender.soma-thetrip: Progressive house and psychedelic trance in the long build that was standard in British clubs in the nineties. Tracks that take ten minutes and use every one of them.
sender.dunkerque-street: From a North Sea port town nobody associates with club music — exactly why. Electro, house, and techno from people who live there and have no scene at their backs.
sender.soma-covers: Exclusively cover versions — and specifically ones that rebuild the original instead of replaying it: punk as bossa nova, rap as bluegrass. A whole channel that lives off the joy of misunderstanding.
sender.soma-insound: Mod jazz, soul jazz, and European film music from the sixties — the music of coffeehouses before it turned into lounge kitsch. Closer to Blue Note than easy listening, with a feel for the moments when both were the same thing.
sender.soma-bossa: Bossa nova and what came after, including modern Brazilian electronic music and European arrangements. Considerably broader than pure bossa stations, which makes it the more interesting address for a genre that otherwise turns into wallpaper fast.
sender.tsf-jazz: The Paris jazz station, a fixture in France. Hosted throughout, with a preference for what's just come out — not an archive station, but one that keeps up with what's happening in the clubs.
sender.concertzender-jazz: The Dutch Concertzender is made by volunteers and funds itself without advertising. The jazz channel is correspondingly headstrong: shows that follow an idea instead of a playlist, often an hour long on a single musician.
sender.radio-swiss-jazz: The jazz channel of Swiss public broadcasting, ad-free and unhosted — music plays, nothing else. The most unruffled way to have jazz running in the background without anyone talking over it.
sender.jazzradio-hu: Out of Budapest, and one of the very few stations broadcasting in Ogg Vorbis instead of MP3 — audibly cleaner in the highs at the same bitrate. Hungarian jazz turns up here more often than elsewhere.
sender.xjazz-movin-grooves: The groove channel of Berlin's XJAZZ Festival, at 320 kbit/s one of the best-sounding jazz streams around. Jazz with a pulse: jazz-funk, broken beat, tracks where the bass sets the direction.
sender.xjazz-electronic: The channel where jazz and electronic music don't alternate but interpenetrate — improvised music with machines inside it. If you're at home in the Engine Room but still miss horns, start here.
sender.le-grigri: A small French station throwing African music, free jazz, and hip-hop into the same pot and stirring. Exactly the kind of neighborhood where genre mixes come about that nobody else would play.
sender.klcbs-fusion: KLCBS calls itself “The Jazz Wave” and broadcasts from Bandung on Java. The fusion channel plays what counts as jazz in Indonesia — and that's considerably closer to Weather Report than to Wynton Marsalis.
sender.wwoz: New Orleans's community radio, carried by listeners and volunteer hosts. Not a jazz station in the museum sense, but the station of a city where jazz is functional music — brass bands, funk, and everything that comes with it.
sender.wnur: Student radio near Chicago, famous for decades for two things: its jazz programming and “Streetbeat.” If you want to hear what a station sounds like when nobody's telling it what to play, listen in here.
sender.radio-unisinos: University radio from southern Brazil. Bossa nova and Brazilian music, but broadcast from the country itself instead of a European lounge channel — the difference is noticeable after two tracks.
sender.kmhd2: The second channel of Portland's jazz station, listener-supported and ad-free. Where the main channel plays the standards, this one goes further out — to where jazz stops following rules.
sender.soma-brfm: The radio of the Burning Man festival in the Nevada desert, which keeps broadcasting for the rest of the year. A mix of desert techno, announcements to a city that only exists one week a year, and things hard to classify.
sender.nts-poolside: The sunniest of the NTS endless mixes: Balearic, boogie, Brazilian material from the seventies, Italian synth-pop. Sounds like late afternoon by the water without tipping into chillout kitsch.
sender.the-lot-radio: Broadcasts from a converted shipping container on a former parking lot in Brooklyn. Guests on the decks around the clock, no programming in the usual sense — you hear whoever happens to be there.
sender.pbs-fm: Community radio from Melbourne, carried by members and volunteer hosts. Australia has a scene Europe barely hears about — it plays here, alongside soul, dub, and whatever people bring in.
sender.wruw: Student radio from Cleveland with the motto “More Diversity, Less Commercials.” Over a hundred shows from volunteers, from polka to noise — the kind of programming no algorithm would ever put together.
sender.nts-labyrinth: The most unwieldy NTS mix: musique concrète, noise, electroacoustic experiments, and things you're not sure qualify as music. Expressly meant as an imposition, and a successful one.
sender.gutsy-radio: Freeform in the original sense: no format, no playlist, no program grid. What plays is decided by whoever's on the mic — and you notice immediately when they change.
sender.nts-otaku: NTS with a British eye on Japanese music — city pop, video game sounds, Japanese ambient and noise in one endless mix. Sorted differently than Japanese stations, because here it's selected rather than maintained.
sender.somafm-u80s: Early UK synth-pop and new wave away from the rotation — Soft Cell, Human League, and plenty that nobody played even back then. SomaFM has funded itself through donations for over twenty years and broadcasts without a single second of advertising as a result.
sender.new-wave-radio: The more accessible side of new wave: Cure, Kate Bush, Duran Duran instead of rarities. If Underground 80s has too much unfamiliar material for you, this is the right place. The website carries ads; whether the stream itself does could not be determined.
sender.italopower: Italo disco, Hi-NRG, and spacesynth — the niche nobody else in the shop covers. New productions in the same style are mixed in, barely distinguishable from the originals. The website funds itself through ads.
sender.rautemusik-80s: The decade's broad hits, no pretense of discovery — the counterpart to Underground 80s and Italopower. RauteMusik has broadcast from Cologne since 2003, and the individual channels run without ad breaks.
sender.rautemusik-90s: Same principle, one decade later: nineties pop and charts, broad rather than curated. Fills the gap that would otherwise sit open between Eurodance and grunge. If you want to hear the nineties as a whole rather than sliced by genre, this is the place.
sender.rautemusik-trance: Trance from the nineties to today — so not just the rearview mirror. Still one of the cleanest freely available sources for Robert Miles, Paul van Dyk, and Cosmic Gate, and without ad breaks.
sender.181fm-oldschool: Wu-Tang, A Tribe Called Quest, TLC, Boyz II Men — the hip-hop and R&B side of the nineties that was missing from the shop entirely until now. Just short station IDs instead of ad blocks. The station has run out of Virginia since 2001 and has preserved the sound of the era instead of polishing it up.
sender.181fm-90salt: Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Stone Temple Pilots. Guitars as a counterweight to a shelf that would otherwise list heavily electronic. Recordings from the years a regional Seattle scene became world music within months.
sender.1fm-90s-best: Broad nineties pop music from Switzerland, and at 256 kbit/s the best-sounding entry on this shelf. 1.FM has broadcast since the earliest days of web radio. From boy bands to Britpop, without the scissors other stations take to anything that doesn't sound catchy today.
sender.90s90s-eurodance: 2 Unlimited, Snap!, Culture Beat, Dr. Alban — Eurodance with no apology. Exactly the genre that divides opinion and that hadn't shown up in the shop before. Music that lived off cheap synthesizers, rapped verses, and sung choruses — and ruled the charts for half a decade.
sender.90s90s-grunge: The same genre as 181.FM 90s Alternative, but from a German vantage point and with a different rotation. Listen to both side by side and you'll quickly notice how differently the same decade gets remembered.
sender.90s90s-rave: The early nineties, when rave still sounded like a warehouse and not a festival stage. Acid house and hardcore before Eurodance and long before trance. Tracks built for sound systems that could barely handle the bass — and that's exactly where their hardness comes from.
sender.soma-seventies: Californian rock and yacht rock from the seventies, curated rather than rotated — Steely Dan next to names that never made it into a best-of compilation. At 320 kbit/s, one of the best-sounding channels in the whole shop.
sender.cowabunga: Northern soul, boogaloo, garage, and power pop from a Spanish collective. Music that flopped in the sixties and got rediscovered decades later on British dance floors — the second career of poorly selling records.
sender.xraydio-jukebox: A Bulgarian jukebox with mod, vintage soul, and jet-set lounge. Sounds like a bar where the records haven't been swapped out since 1966 — which is exactly the appeal of this selection.
sender.xraydio-live: The broader sister channel: garage punk, dream pop, acid house, and Americana in the same program. A station that refuses to make up its mind and stays surprisingly coherent anyway.
sender.wraith-vision: Doo-wop, crooners, and rhythm and blues from the fifties and sixties. The music pop music started with, played without the nostalgia filter oldies stations usually lay over it — as if the recordings had just come out.
sender.rsa-ostrock: Rock music from East Germany — Puhdys, Karat, Silly, City. A music history that ran parallel to the Western one for forty years and that almost nobody outside East Germany knows to this day.
sender.france-musique: The classical channel of French public broadcasting, with its own orchestras and live broadcasts from the Auditorium. Broadcasts in a hi-fi version at 48 kHz — audibly more space than the usual 44.1.
sender.swiss-classic: Ad-free, license-fee funded, classical around the clock with no hosting between pieces. At 192 kbit/s AAC, one of the cleanest freely available classical streams around. No talk segment interrupts, no jingle — the music plays until it's over.
sender.czro-ddur: The classical channel of Czech public broadcasting, with a conspicuous amount of Czech repertoire — Janáček, Martinů, Suk. Composers who rarely get past Dvořák in German-language programming.
sender.br-klassik: With its own symphony orchestra and choir, whose recordings run regularly in the program. Talk segments between pieces explain what's coming next — the kind of radio where you learn something on the side.
sender.ndr-kultur: Classical with literature, radio drama, and conversation mixed in. If you want music without a single word, Radio Swiss Classic is the better fit — here, talking is part of the program. A culture station in the old sense, treating music and language as belonging together.
sender.oe1: The culture station of Austrian public broadcasting, since 1967. Classical, new music, science, and features in one program — an institution in Vienna, barely known outside it. A station you switch on and end up having heard something other than what you planned.
sender.kusc: The largest listener-funded classical station in the US, backed by a university in Los Angeles. American classical radio sounds more approachable than European — less reverence, more storytelling.
sender.wqxr: New York's classical station since 1936, once owned by the New York Times, now listener-funded. Regularly broadcasts from Carnegie Hall and the city's orchestras. The best address in the catalog for American orchestras and American composers.
sender.venice-classic: A small Venetian station focused on baroque and Italian repertoire — Vivaldi, Albinoni, Marcello, in their own city. Ad-free and unhosted. If you want to hear baroque as repertoire rather than background, this is where the depth is.
sender.early-music: Exclusively early music: medieval, Renaissance, early baroque, on period instruments. The counterpart to Ancient FM over in Curiosities — same field, different hand. Music from centuries when concert pitch wasn't yet fixed at 440 Hz.
sender.walm2-opus: Classical off original shellac records, broadcast in Opus at 192 kbit/s. The same people who run Adroit Jazz over on the jazz shelf — you hear the record, not the remastered reissue.
sender.flowstate-classical: Classical at 320 kbit/s and 48 kHz, selected for long, focused listening rather than the quick climax. The best-sounding entry on this shelf after WALM. Long movements stay whole instead of being trimmed for attention spans.
sender.fine-music-radio: Classical and jazz from Cape Town, made by volunteers. The only station on this shelf that plays both on equal footing — and the only one from the African continent.
